units.text: Prologue. The morning it falls differently

Imagine that tomorrow morning a laboratory announces something almost ridiculous: two highly precise clocks operating through different mechanisms no longer maintain the same ratio between their rates. The team checks temperature, power supply and analysis software. Then it replaces the instruments. The difference remains. Other laboratories reproduce the observation. It is not a fluke, but nobody yet knows what it is.

One news story will say the laws of nature have changed. Another, that the universe has received an update. A cautious physicist will say something has changed in the relationship between measurements and model. The three sentences do not carry the same weight. The first interprets; the second, for now, invents a cause; the third defines a problem.

The scene is imaginary. Its question is real: what would have to happen for the expression ‘law of nature’ to lose its meaning? A single deviation? A century of different regularities? The discovery of deeper rules? Or the discovery of a programmer?

We are accustomed to saying that the universe obeys laws. The verb hides a small drama. Obeying a human law presupposes that violating it is possible. A pedestrian can cross against a red light. An electron does not seem to choose between obedience and revolt. When a result contradicts a physical law, we usually do not put the electron on trial: we check the law, conditions and measurement.

Yet the idea of law does something extraordinary. It allows us to use what has happened to anticipate what has not happened yet. It transforms experience into a transmissible resource. At the same time, it can turn a habit into destiny: ‘That is human nature’, ‘That is how the market works’, ‘The weak always lose’. Sometimes we know a constraint. At other times we hide behind it.

This book follows both powers of the concept. The first builds tools, explanations and possibilities for intervention. The second closes discussions before they begin. We have no reason to confuse them or to give up the first because we fear the second.

We will also reach a possibility seemingly taken from cinema: a simulated world capable of discovering that it is simulated. The interesting problem is not whether we can invent such a story. We can invent countless ones. The problem is whether the story bears the risk of being wrong and whether observations exist that separate it from competing explanations.

Our starting position is deliberately modest: the world can contradict us. It does not follow that we know what its laws ultimately are. It does follow, however, that the difference between a good explanation and a convenient one matters. Perhaps the universe contains no sentences. But some of our sentences survive encounters with it much better than others.
